definition: An embedding turns a word, sentence, or document into a long list of numbers — a position in 'meaning space.' Words with similar meanings end up close together: 'king' and 'queen' are neighbors, 'king' and 'carburetor' are far apart. It's how AI matches on meaning instead of matching on exact letters.

edges.label: numbers behind
edges.note: Tokens are the text chunks; embeddings are their numeric form.

edges.label: power RAG search
edges.note: Retrieval finds relevant documents by embedding similarity.

example.body: You search the help center for 'how do I reset my password' and the top result is titled 'credential recovery process.' Zero words in common, perfect match — because in meaning space, those two phrases are neighbors. Old keyword search would have found nothing.
example.title: The password article with no 'password' in it

footnotes.body: Embeddings are dense vectors — typically hundreds to thousands of dimensions — produced by a trained encoder model. Similarity is measured with cosine similarity or dot product. The same machinery powers semantic search, recommendations, clustering, and duplicate detection.
footnotes.label: For the technical reader

name: Embeddings
tagline: Words turned into numbers, so the AI can tell which ideas are close in meaning.
whyItMatters: Embeddings are the quiet engine behind search that 'just gets it.' When a search finds the right help article even though you used completely different words, embeddings did that. They also power RAG, recommendations, and duplicate detection — most of the AI features that feel magical are embeddings plus a database.
